967.title: Exchanging self and other
967.hook: Shantideva: put yourself in another's place, completely
967.howItsDone: In Tibetan Buddhism, exchanging self and other is taught from the eighth chapter of Shantideva's Bodhicaryavatara, and it underlies mind-training practices in which practitioners imagine taking on others' suffering and giving away their own happiness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lazy monk: Shantideva, thought to do nothing but eat and sleep, stood up and recited a masterpiece. Your line was the lazy one spoke. Whom did you surprise? Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

A stubbed toe. The hand goes straight down to it. Nobody tells the hand to do that, and the hand never stops to ask what the foot has done for it lately. It just goes, because the hand and the foot belong to one body. In the masterpiece the lazy monk recited, the guide to the bodhisattva's way of life, there's a chapter on meditation that takes that ordinary reflex and pushes it as far as it will go. What if the line around the body were drawn somewhere else? Today: exchanging self and other.
screen: `THE HAND GOES TO THE FOOT.` → `ONE BODY.` → `WHAT IF THE LINE MOVED?`

segments.voice: Shantideva builds it in steps. First, the sameness. I want to be happy and I don't want to suffer. So does everyone else, in exactly the same way. If that's true, he asks, what makes my pain the one worth guarding? Only habit. He uses the picture of the body: the hand protects the foot as a part of itself, and so, he says, beings can be cared for as parts of one life. Second, the exchange itself. Having seen that everyone is the same in wanting happiness, he turns it around. Put yourself where the other person stands, and look back. In one passage he has the practitioner take the place of someone worse off, then an equal, then someone better off, and look back at their old self from each seat, calling that old self he. From the other side of the table, my own pride looks very different. Third, why bother. Shantideva is blunt about it: the misery in the world comes from wanting happiness only for oneself, and the joy in the world comes from wishing others well. He calls this exchange a supreme secret, a practice for those who want to protect themselves and others quickly. Fourth, what it isn't. It isn't erasing yourself, or pretending you have no needs. The practitioner still eats and sleeps. It's a shift of where the center sits, practiced on purpose, the way a musician practices scales. Tibetan teachers later built whole trainings on this chapter. In these verses his tone is plain and urgent, with nothing sentimental in it.
screen: `EVERYONE WANTS THE SAME THING.` · `STAND THERE AND LOOK BACK.` · `A SUPREME SECRET.` · `NOT ERASING YOURSELF.` · then, large: `EXCHANGE SELF AND OTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: trade places for two minutes. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person you saw yesterday, anyone at all. Now sit where they sat. Feel their chair, their morning, their tiredness, what they were hoping for. From there, look across at yourself. What did they see? Don't judge it. Just look from their side for a while, then come home to your own breath. The bell holds the time.
Exchanging self and other. Shantideva's practice of standing where another stands, wanting their good as if it were your own. Today's word.
Your line: exchange self and other. Today, choose one hour and spend it as someone else: in every small choice, ask what they would need. Day nine hundred sixty-seven.

screen: `DAY 967 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: A LAMP FOR THE PATH.`

968.title: A lamp for the path
968.hook: Atisha's short text sets out the stages of the path
968.howItsDone: Atisha's Lamp for the Path to Awakening is studied in Tibetan monasteries and retreat centers, and its outline of three kinds of practitioner shapes the lamrim, the stages-of-the-path teachings given in Tibetan Buddhist communities.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shantideva's exchange: stand where another stands and look back at yourself. Your line was exchange self and other. Whose hour did you live? Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

A hiker at the edge of a dark trail doesn't need the whole mountain lit up. A small lamp will do, as long as it shows the next few steps and roughly where they lead. We've already met Atisha, the Indian teacher whose coming to Tibet brought a renewal. Tradition says a Tibetan ruler asked him for something simple: not a library, but a guide a person could carry. What Atisha wrote is short. Its title says what it's for. Today: a lamp for the path.
screen: `A SMALL LAMP, A DARK TRAIL.` → `NOT A LIBRARY.` → `A GUIDE YOU CAN CARRY.`

segments.voice: The text is the Lamp for the Path to Awakening. We met its outline when Atisha first came to Tibet. Today, a closer look inside. First, three people. The opening verses sort readers not by school but by aim. Some seek good things for themselves within the round of lives. Some turn from that round toward their own peace. And some want to end the suffering of others as if it were their own. The Lamp says plainly that the rest of it is written for that third person. Second, a wish, then vows. The Lamp asks that person to take refuge and raise the wish to awaken for everyone's sake, the same wish we heard from Shantideva, and then to keep vows. A wish with no conduct behind it stays a wish. Third, the bird. For meditation, Atisha uses a plain picture: a bird whose wings haven't grown can't fly. Without a settled, steady mind, he says, a person can't do much good for others. So calm comes first. Fourth, two wings. Near the end, the Lamp says that wisdom without skillful means is bondage, and skillful means without wisdom is bondage too, so keep both. Insight with no kindness binds; kindness with no insight binds another way. Later Tibetan teachers wrote whole books on this outline, a genre called lamrim, the stages of the path. The Lamp itself is short enough to carry, which was the point. It leaves two questions: what are you aiming at, and has the aim grown its wings?
screen: `THREE PEOPLE, THREE AIMS.` · `A WISH, THEN VOWS.` · `A BIRD WITHOUT WINGS CAN'T FLY.` · `WISDOM AND MEANS, BOTH.` · then, large: `A LAMP FOR THE PATH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your own three steps. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: what do I want for my own life this year? Let one answer come. Breathe. Then ask: what would real peace look like for me, underneath that? Let one answer come. Breathe. Then ask: what would I wish for the people around me, all of them? Let one answer come. Three steps, in your own words. Then rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
A lamp for the path. Atisha's short text that sorts the path by aim: a good life, peace for oneself, and freedom for everyone. Today's word.
screen: `A LAMP FOR THE PATH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: a lamp for the path. Today, write your three steps down on paper, in a few words each, and keep them where you'll see them. Day nine hundred sixty-eight.

969.title: Atisha's cook
969.hook: a legend: Atisha kept a bad-tempered cook as a teacher of patience
969.howItsDone: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Atisha's cook when teaching patience, alongside Shantideva's chapter on patience, and some practitioners deliberately treat difficult people as teachers in their daily mind training.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Atisha's lamp: a small aim, a middle aim, and the great aim of freedom for everyone. Your line was a lamp for the path. Did you write your three steps down? Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

Every kitchen has a temperature, and this one ran hot. The story people tell goes like this. When Atisha traveled to Tibet, he brought along an attendant from India who cooked for him, and this man was difficult: rude, quick to snap, grumbling at everyone, including his teacher. The Tibetans who met him were puzzled. Why would a great master keep a man like that? Surely someone kinder could do the job. Atisha's answer, in the story, is still retold. Today: Atisha's cook.
screen: `A HOT KITCHEN.` → `A RUDE ATTENDANT.` → `WHY KEEP HIM?`

segments.voice: First, the answer. In the legend, Atisha says the cook isn't a servant at all. He's a teacher, the one who teaches patience. Some tellings add a smile: the Tibetans were so gentle that, without the cook, Atisha would have had nothing left to practice on. It's a legend, and it's told with a wink. But it lands on something serious. Second, where the idea comes from. Shantideva's guide, the one we met two days ago, has a whole chapter on patience. There he argues that a person who harms you gives you something no friend can: the chance to practice patience. Without someone difficult, he says, patience has nothing to grow on. He even compares an enemy to a treasure that turns up in your own house, unearned. Third, what the story does with it. Shantideva gives the argument. Atisha's cook puts it in a kitchen, with a face and a bad mood. It's one thing to agree that difficult people teach patience. It's another to keep one on the payroll. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. The story isn't telling anyone to stay in harm's way or accept abuse. Buddhist teachers speak of patience alongside wisdom: seeing clearly what's happening, and refusing to add your own anger to it. The cook is grumpy, not dangerous. Closer to home, there may be a cook somewhere nearby: a coworker, a neighbor, a relative at the holiday table. The legend asks a quiet question. What if that person is the lesson, and not the obstacle to it?
screen: `NOT A SERVANT: A TEACHER.` · `SHANTIDEVA: AN ENEMY IS A TREASURE.` · `THE ARGUMENT, IN A KITCHEN.` · `PATIENCE WITH WISDOM, NOT HARM.` · then, large: `MY TEACHER OF PATIENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: thank a difficult person, silently. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who tests your patience. Not someone who has truly hurt you; just someone who rubs you the wrong way. See their face. If something tightens, in the chest or the jaw, let it be there. Then, on an out-breath, say inwardly: thank you for the practice. You don't have to mean it fully. Just try it a few times, and rest. The bell holds the time.
Atisha's cook. In the legend, a bad-tempered attendant Atisha kept on purpose, calling him his teacher of patience. Today's word.
Your line: my teacher of patience. Today, when someone grates on you, name them that, under your breath, before you answer. Day nine hundred sixty-nine.

no added anger, no staying in harm

970.title: Tilopa and Naropa
970.hook: the scholar Naropa leaves his university post to serve the wild teacher Tilopa
970.howItsDone: In the Kagyu school of Tibetan Buddhism, Tilopa and Naropa are honored at the head of the lineage, and the story of Naropa's search is told to students as a picture of devotion and of the gap between knowing words and knowing their meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the grumpy cook Atisha kept on purpose. Your line was my teacher of patience. Who earned that title from you? Day nine hundred seventy.

Naropa had what scholars dream of. In the stories, he held a high post at Nalanda, a great monastic university in India, where he defended the teaching in debate and could recite texts by the shelf. One day, as he sat reading, a shadow fell across the page. An old woman, bent and ugly in the telling, asked him a question. Do you understand the words, or the meaning? Naropa said: the words. She laughed with delight. Then he added: and the meaning. And she wept. Today: Tilopa and Naropa.
screen: `A SCHOLAR AT NALANDA.` → `A SHADOW ON THE PAGE.` → `WORDS, OR MEANING?`

segments.voice: First, the question. In Tibetan tellings, the old woman is a dakini, a wisdom figure in disguise. Her laughter and her tears say it all: Naropa knew the words; he did not yet know the meaning. When he asked who did, she named Tilopa. Second, the leaving. Naropa gave up his post and went looking. The stories make this hard. He finds Tilopa nowhere and everywhere: in strange people on the road who disgust him, whom he refuses to help, and who turn out, too late, to have been Tilopa all along. Third, the teacher. When Naropa finally finds him, Tilopa looks nothing like a professor. In some tellings he's a wild man by a river, living on scraps of fish. He doesn't lecture. He sets Naropa trials, one after another, many of them painful and some frightening, and teaches through each one in a few words. Fourth, the turn. The legend is extreme, and Kagyu tellings hold it up as a picture of devotion to a teacher. What it carries is a reversal. The celebrated scholar becomes the servant of someone with no titles, because that person knows the meaning. In the Kagyu tradition, Tilopa and Naropa stand at the head of a lineage, teacher to student, that we will follow over the coming days. Away from Nalanda, the story has a gentler edge. Knowing the words is good. Somewhere near you, someone with no credentials may know the meaning.
screen: `THE DAKINI LAUGHS, THEN WEEPS.` · `NAROPA LEAVES HIS POST.` · `A WILD TEACHER BY THE RIVER.` · `THE SCHOLAR BECOMES THE SERVANT.` · then, large: `THE SCHOLAR SERVED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look for the unexpected teacher. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind move through the people you'll meet today, or met yesterday: the bus driver, the child, the person at the register, the neighbor you never talk to. Pause on one. Ask: what might this person know that I don't? Don't answer too quickly. Let the question sit with you, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Tilopa and Naropa. The wild teacher and the great scholar who left everything to serve him. Today's word.
Your line: the scholar served. Today, learn one thing from someone you wouldn't usually ask, and tell them thank you. Day nine hundred seventy.

971.title: Marpa
971.hook: the farmer-translator who walked to India three times for the teachings
971.howItsDone: In the Kagyu school, Marpa is honored as the translator who brought Naropa's teachings to Tibet, and his image, often shown as a stocky layman rather than a monk, appears in Kagyu lineage paintings and prayers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the scholar Naropa left his post to find the wild teacher Tilopa. Your line was the scholar served. Who taught you something unexpected? Day nine hundred seventy-one.

He wasn't a monk. He had a wife, a farm, fields to watch and a temper to match. He liked his beer, the stories say. And Tibetans remember him with deep honor. His name was Marpa, and he became known as Marpa the Translator. Tradition says he made the trip from Tibet over the Himalaya to India three times, on foot, to find teachers and bring their words home. Today: Marpa.
screen: `NOT A MONK.` → `A FARMER WITH A TEMPER.` → `MARPA THE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: First, the cost. The teachings weren't free, and the road was dangerous: mountain passes, fevers in the hot plains below, robbers. In the stories, Marpa turned what he owned into gold to offer his teachers, and walked. Second, the teacher. In India he found Naropa, yesterday's scholar, now a master himself, and studied with him and others. He learned the language well enough to carry not only texts but their meaning, which yesterday's story says is the hard part. Third, the return. Each time, he came back to Tibet and worked: translating, teaching, farming. He didn't shave his head or enter a monastery. He showed that a householder could carry a lineage, with a family and a farm around him. Fourth, the going back. Why go again? Tradition gives more than one reason: to fill gaps, to receive teachings he had missed, to see his teacher once more. Marpa got enough to be a respected teacher at home, and still went back, because enough wasn't the point. The Kagyu tradition remembers him as the link between Naropa in India and the Tibetan students who came after. One of them, Milarepa, will fill the next several days of this path, and Marpa will turn out to be a fierce and strange teacher. Marpa's journeys leave a plain question. What would you walk a long way for? Not buy, not download. Walk for, and come back with, and then walk for again.
screen: `GOLD FOR THE TEACHERS.` · `NAROPA, IN INDIA.` · `A HOUSEHOLDER CARRIES IT HOME.` · `AND HE WENT BACK AGAIN.` · then, large: `THREE JOURNEYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find your long road. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: what is worth real effort to me? A skill, a relationship, a question, a practice. Let one thing come. Picture the first stretch of the road toward it: one concrete step, small enough to take this week. See yourself taking it. Then rest, and let the breath carry you, step by step. The bell holds the time.
Marpa. The farmer and householder who, tradition says, walked to India three times and carried the teaching home as a translator. Today's word.
Your line: three journeys. Today, go the distance for one thing: the extra mile, the second draft, the call you'd normally skip. Day nine hundred seventy-one.

972.title: Milarepa's remorse
972.hook: Milarepa used black magic to take revenge, then turned to the teaching in remorse
972.howItsDone: Milarepa's life story is read and retold in Tibetan Buddhist communities, and teachers use its opening, revenge and remorse, to show that even serious wrongdoing can be turned from through regret, purification and practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marpa the farmer-translator, walking to India and back for the teaching. Your line was three journeys. What did you go the distance for? Day nine hundred seventy-two.

A saint Tibetans hold dear begins his story as a killer. That's not a rumor; it's how his life story tells it. Milarepa was a boy when his father died. His uncle and aunt took charge of the family's fields and house, promising to hand them back when the boy grew up. They didn't. The widow and her children were left to work as servants on their own land, in rags. His mother never forgot it. And when Milarepa was grown, she put a demand to him that would change everything. Today: Milarepa's remorse.
screen: `A FATHER DIES.` → `AN UNCLE TAKES THE FIELDS.` → `A MOTHER'S DEMAND.`

segments.voice: First, the revenge. His mother sent him to learn black magic, and told him, in the story, that if he failed she would take her own life. He learned it. At the uncle's house, during a wedding feast, the building collapsed and many guests died, though the uncle and aunt survived. His mother rejoiced. When the villagers turned against her, he called down a hailstorm on their fields. Second, the turn. Milarepa didn't. The biography says he was filled with remorse: he couldn't sleep, couldn't eat, couldn't stop seeing what he had done. In Buddhist teaching, actions bring their results, and he knew that what he had set in motion would follow him. Third, what remorse does here. It doesn't stop at guilt. Guilt can just sit on a person. Milarepa's remorse got up and went looking. He sought out a teacher, then another, and finally heard the name Marpa, and the story says the name alone moved him to tears. Fourth, why the story starts there. Tibetans could have told the life of a saint who was always good. Instead they keep the worst part in, at the start, in full. As teachers tell it, the message is plain: no one is too far gone to turn back. The harm is real; the story never pretends otherwise. But the turn is real too. Milarepa will spend years paying for what he did, as we'll see tomorrow. The question it leaves is a small one. Not what's the worst thing you've done, but where is one harm you could stop today, and turn from?
screen: `BLACK MAGIC, AT HIS MOTHER'S DEMAND.` · `REMORSE: NO SLEEP, NO FOOD.` · `REMORSE THAT GOES LOOKING.` · `THE WORST PART, KEPT IN.` · then, large: `HE TURNED BACK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: turn from one harm. Settle, and breathe. Without digging for anything heavy, notice one small way you've been causing harm lately: a sharp tone, a habit, a word about someone behind their back. Name it plainly to yourself. If there's a sting, let it be there, without flinching. Then picture yourself turning, the way a person turns on a road. One harm, set down. Rest in the breath. The bell holds the time.
Milarepa's remorse. The sorrow over his revenge that didn't stop at guilt, but sent him looking for a teacher. Today's word.
Your line: he turned back. Today, stop one small harm for a full day, and notice what it's like without it. Day nine hundred seventy-two.

973.title: The towers
973.hook: Marpa has him build towers and tear them down, again and again
973.howItsDone: Tibetan teachers tell the story of Milarepa's towers as a teaching on purifying past harm and on perseverance, and in the Kagyu tradition a tower in southern Tibet is honored as the one tradition says Milarepa finally completed for Marpa's son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Milarepa's revenge, and the remorse that sent him looking for a teacher. Your line was he turned back. Which harm did you set down? Day nine hundred seventy-three.

Milarepa finally finds Marpa, the farmer-translator, plowing a field. He bows and asks for the teaching. He offers himself, body, speech and mind. And Marpa, the great teacher he has wept just to hear named, says something like this: fine, but you can't have food and teaching both. Choose. Milarepa has nothing to offer but his own two hands. So Marpa points to a ridge and gives him a job. Build me a tower. Today: the towers.
screen: `MILAREPA FINDS MARPA.` → `FOOD OR TEACHING: CHOOSE.` → `BUILD ME A TOWER.`

segments.voice: First, the building. Milarepa hauls stones on his back and builds the tower, alone. When it's partly done, Marpa comes to look and says he wasn't thinking clearly when he asked for it. Tear it down, and put every stone back where you found it. Second, again. A new spot, a new shape, a new tower. Again Marpa changes his mind. Again it comes down. The story repeats it, and each time, Milarepa's back grows more raw from the stones, and still no teaching comes. Third, the hidden kindness. Marpa's wife, Dagmema, sees it all and pleads for him. She even helps him with a trick to win some teaching from another student, which Marpa later uncovers. Milarepa despairs and nearly gives up. Fourth, what it was for. In the story, Marpa finally explains. The towers were never about towers. Milarepa had done terrible harm, and the endless labor, borne without anger, was a way to purify it. Marpa's harshness, he says, was itself the teaching. Then, at last, he accepts Milarepa as his student. The story is extreme, and it is about one student with one past; it is no rulebook for how a teacher may treat anyone. What it offers the rest of us is the rhythm: build, take it down, build again, without bitterness. And a look back at the week. Shantideva taught us to exchange self and other. Atisha lit a lamp for the path, and kept a cook for patience. Naropa left his post to serve Tilopa. Marpa walked to India and back. Milarepa turned from harm. Today, he picks up the first stone.
screen: `BUILD IT. TEAR IT DOWN.` · `AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` · `DAGMEMA PLEADS FOR HIM.` · `THE LABOR WAS THE TEACHING.` · then, large: `BUILD IT AGAIN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: begin again, without bitterness. Settle, and breathe. Notice your attention. Sooner or later it will wander off, to a plan, a worry, a sound. When you notice, don't scold it. Just set the stone down where you found it, and come back to the breath, like starting a new tower. Again. And again. Each return is the practice, not a failure of it. The bell holds the time.

fork.setup: you're Milarepa. you've built a tower for Marpa, your back is raw, and he tells you to tear it down and put the stones back. what do you do?
options: refuse and leave.
tear it down and build again.
argue until he admits he's wrong.
fork.reveal: Milarepa tore it down and built again, more than once, before Marpa finally accepted him.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cruel teacher playing games.
what it means: in the story, the endless building and unbuilding was how Milarepa purified the harm he had done.
what a scholar hears: the hardship itself named as the teaching, and Marpa's wife Dagmema as the voice of mercy beside it.
